summary: One of the periodic IAB status reports on which Internet protocols were at which stage of standardization. It gives an overview of procedures and the RFC series, explains terms, and lists protocols. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1130.

eli5.summary: A school keeps a chart saying which lessons are finished and which are still being worked on. This is a copy of that chart for Internet rules, later replaced by a newer one.

questions: what does experimental mean for a protocol
subtitle: The IAB's framework for standardizing Internet protocols

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a way to track which protocols were official standards, which were being tested, and which were obsolete or experimental.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Activities Board published a periodic memo describing every protocol's standardization state (like proposed, draft, or standard) and its status (like required or elective).
tldr.outcome: This document became the official reference for protocol status. It was regularly updated and later replaced by RFC 1130 with clearer definitions.

today: RFC 1100 is a Historic document. It was replaced by RFC 1130, which provided clearer and more detailed explanations of the standardization process and the different categories of protocols.

sections.title: Purpose and Context
sections.content:
RFC 1100 is an official memo from the Internet Activities Board (IAB) that describes the standardization state of every known Internet protocol. It serves as the authoritative reference for determining which protocols are official standards, which are proposed or experimental, and which are obsolete.

The memo emphasizes that the IAB maintains this list to coordinate the evolution of Internet protocols in a time when they are increasingly in commercial use. Protocol proposals come from anyone in the Internet community by writing and submitting an RFC, but the IAB assigns them to working groups for review before deciding on their status.
sections.eli5: This is the official list of which Internet rules are done, in progress, or retired. The Internet Activities Board publishes it to keep everyone on the same page.

sections.title: The Standardization Process
sections.content:
Internet protocols move through a sequence of states. A proposed protocol begins in the proposed state, where it is implemented and tested by several groups. Once it becomes stable and has a sponsor (someone willing to represent it to the IAB), it advances to draft standard status. A draft standard stays in this state for at least six months to allow the Internet community to find flaws. Finally, if no serious objections emerge, the IAB designates it a standard.

Protocols that are outdated or unused are declared historic. The RFC text explains that some protocols have become important to the Internet community through widespread implementation even without IAB approval, but the IAB reserves the term standard for protocols it has officially approved.

Experimental protocols are research efforts not intended for operational use. A system should not implement an experimental protocol unless coordinated with the protocol's developer.
sections.eli5: Protocols start as ideas, get tested, then become official if they work well. Old ones are marked retired. The IAB decides which are official and which are just experiments.

sections.title: State and Status: Two Dimensions
sections.content:
Every protocol has two independent classifications. The first is its standardization state: standard, draft standard, proposed, experimental, or historic. The second is its requirement status: required, recommended, elective, or not recommended.

A protocol's requirement status indicates how widely it should be deployed. Required protocols must be implemented in all Internet systems. Recommended protocols should be implemented. Elective protocols may be implemented if needed for a particular system's functionality. Not recommended protocols are discouraged for general use, typically because they are experimental or historic.

The RFC includes a matrix showing that most protocols cluster on the main diagonal: standards are usually required or recommended, while proposed protocols are elective or not recommended. Few protocols are required in all systems because the Internet has diverse hardware: gateways, terminal servers, workstations, and hosts have different needs. However, a general-purpose host is expected to implement IP (including ICMP), TCP, UDP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, Mail, and DNS.
sections.eli5: Every protocol has two labels: is it finished (standard) or still being tested (proposed)? And how important is it: must everyone use it (required) or is it optional (elective)?

sections.title: The RFC Document Series
sections.content:
The RFC series is the main publication channel for Internet research and development. An RFC can cover nearly any topic related to computer communication: meeting reports, protocol specifications, experimental results, and standards. Anyone can submit a document for publication as an RFC; submissions go by electronic mail to the RFC Editor.

The RFC text stresses an important principle: once an RFC is assigned a number and published, it is never revised or re-issued with that same number. This means there is never ambiguity about which version you have. However, a protocol (such as FTP) can be described in multiple RFCs over time as it improves. This memo serves as the reference for determining which RFC describes the current specification of each protocol.
sections.eli5: RFCs are documents anyone can write and publish about Internet ideas. Once published with a number, that document never changes. This memo tells you which RFC has the latest version of each protocol.

sections.title: Reference Documents and Further Information
sections.content:
RFC 1100 points to several companion documents. Assigned Numbers (RFC 1010) lists the numeric values used by protocols, such as IP protocol codes and TCP port numbers. The Official Protocols document (RFC 1011) describes protocols and any known problems. Gateway Requirements (RFC 1009) clarifies specifications for routers, and Host Requirements (in preparation) will do the same for end systems.

The RFC also notes that DoD MIL-STD specifications exist for IP and TCP alongside the Internet RFCs, and both should be used together since they differ in style and detail. FTP, SMTP, and Telnet have comparable MIL-STD versions.
sections.eli5: Other documents list the protocol numbers, describe problems, and explain what routers and computers must do. The military also has versions of some protocols.
